opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think a lot of what we've learned from coding agents carries over pretty directly, but with some important caveats.

The reason coding has been such a productive testbed is that it has a few really nice properties. You have a well-defined environment, the codebase, the terminal, the tools. You have fairly crisp feedback signals: does it compile, do the tests pass, does the program do what you expected. And the actions are mostly reversible. You can run something, see that it failed, and try again. That loop of act, observe, correct is what lets these models do long-horizon work, and it's why we've seen such rapid progress there.

When you move to enterprise or consumer workflows, the core principles still hold. You want the model to be able to plan, break a task into steps, call tools, read the results, and recover from its own mistakes. You want it to manage context well over a long task, knowing what to keep, what to summarize, and what to go back and look up. Those capabilities are fairly general, and a lot of what we train for in coding transfers.

What's different is the environment. In an enterprise setting, the "tools" are things like CRMs, ticketing systems, spreadsheets, internal APIs, email. They're messier, less documented, and often not designed to be used by an agent. The feedback signal is also much fuzzier. There's no unit test that tells you whether you handled a customer escalation well or drafted the right summary for an executive. So you need to think much harder about evaluation, about building verifiers or rubrics that approximate what "correct" looks like for that workflow.

The other big difference is reversibility and stakes. If a coding agent writes a bad function, you revert the commit. If an agent sends the wrong email to a customer or moves money incorrectly, that's much harder to undo. So the design of these agents has to include a clear notion of when to act autonomously and when to check in with the human. I think that's one of the most important lessons: the agent needs to understand which actions are cheap to try and which ones need confirmation.

On the consumer side, there's also personalization and trust. People's preferences are implicit, and the agent has to learn them without being annoying, asking just enough questions to get it right but not so many that it's easier to do the task yourself.

So my short answer is that coding agents gave us the blueprint: tight feedback loops, good tool use, long-horizon planning, and self-correction. The work now is building environments and evaluations for these other domains that are as rich as what we have in code, and designing the human-in-the-loop pieces so people can actually trust these systems with real work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses coding agents and workflow agents, but does not attribute multimodal reasoning to large-scale pre-training.

r002.rationale: It says coding-agent capabilities and principles transfer across domains, naming planning, tool use, context management, and self-correction as general capabilities.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that adapting these principles mainly requires changing the final stage of post-training.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because coding agents are really the first place where agents have genuinely worked, and the question is what transfers.

The way I'd frame it is that coding happened to have three things lined up at once. First, there's a verifiable signal. You write code, you run the tests, the compiler tells you whether it's right. That gives you a feedback loop that the agent can use at inference time, and that we can use at training time to actually improve the model. Second, the environment is richly tool-equipped. You have a terminal, a file system, a search tool, a debugger. The agent can act, observe, and act again. And third, the people building these tools were also the users, so the loop between "this feels wrong" and "let's fix the scaffolding" was incredibly tight.

When you move to enterprise or consumer workflows, the model capabilities carry over, but those three conditions often don't. The hard part isn't the planning or the reasoning. It's that verification gets fuzzy. If I'm an agent processing an insurance claim or drafting a customer response, there's no unit test that tells me I got it right. So a lot of the work becomes: how do you construct a proxy for that signal? Sometimes that's rubrics, sometimes it's structured outputs that a downstream system can validate, sometimes it's a human in the loop at specific checkpoints rather than everywhere.

The second thing that transfers is the importance of the harness. In coding, we learned that the model is maybe half the story and the environment design is the other half. What tools does the agent have, how is context managed over a long task, when does it ask for clarification versus proceed. Those lessons apply directly. Enterprise systems have the equivalent of a terminal, it's just APIs, databases, ticketing systems. The work is in exposing those in a way that's legible to the model and safe to act on.

And then there's a principle I'd call reversibility. Coding agents got away with a lot because git exists. You can try something, see it fail, roll back. Most enterprise actions aren't like that. Sending an email, moving money, updating a customer record, those are one-way doors. So I think the design pattern shifts toward agents that do a lot of reading, drafting, and simulating, and then present a small number of irreversible actions for confirmation. That's not a limitation of the model, it's just the right architecture for the domain.

The consumer side is interesting for a different reason. The task is often underspecified. "Plan my trip" has no ground truth. So the agent has to be good at eliciting preferences and showing its work in a way that lets the person steer. That's actually something coding agents are now getting better at too, this idea of checking in at the right moments rather than either asking constantly or going off for twenty minutes and coming back with the wrong thing.

So I'd say: the core loop of plan, act, observe, correct is universal. What changes is where the feedback comes from and how expensive a mistake is. Getting those two things right for each domain is most of the work.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss reasoning across modalities or attribute it to large-scale pre-training.

r002.rationale: It says model capabilities carry over, identifies planning and reasoning as shared capabilities, and calls the plan–act–observe–correct loop universal across domains.

r003.rationale: It discusses adapting feedback, tools, and safeguards, but does not say adaptation primarily requires changing the final stage of post-training.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of the principles carry over. With a coding agent, you have a goal, you have tools to interact with an environment, and you have some way to check whether you’re making progress. The agent can make a change, run a test, look at the result, and decide what to do next. That cycle is useful well beyond coding.

For an enterprise workflow, the tools might be a database, a document system, or a business application. But the agent still needs to understand the task, find the relevant context, take an action, and verify the outcome. One challenge is that verification can be much less clear. A test passing gives you a useful signal in coding. How do you establish that a customer issue was actually resolved, rather than just that a response was sent?

And for consumer workflows, understanding the user’s preferences becomes particularly important. If I ask an agent to plan a trip, there are many possible answers, and the agent needs to know when it has enough information to act and when it should ask me.

So I would carry over that iterative approach, but design the feedback and the boundaries around the particular workflow. What can the agent check? What can it do independently? Where does it need human input? Those questions are central to making it useful and reliable.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss multimodal reasoning or attribute it to large-scale pre-training.

r002.rationale: It says coding-agent principles carry over to enterprise and consumer workflows, but does not identify cross-domain reasoning as their shared foundation.

r003.rationale: The response discusses adapting feedback and boundaries to each workflow, but does not mention post-training or changing its final stage.

sol-6.1.text:
I think coding is a useful starting point because it gives an agent a concrete feedback loop. It can make a change, run a test, look at the result, and revise its approach. For enterprise and consumer workflows, we need to think about what the equivalent feedback loop looks like. How does the agent know that it has actually accomplished what the user wanted?

The underlying capabilities are very similar: understanding the goal, breaking it into steps, using tools, and adapting when something goes wrong. But the environment can be much less explicit. A user might ask you to organize a trip or help with a business process, and there are preferences, permissions, and constraints that aren’t all captured in the initial request.

So the challenge is to give the agent enough context and reliable ways to check its work, while making good decisions about when to act and when to ask the user. You can automate more as those feedback mechanisms become stronger. I think that’s the broader lesson from coding agents: the model matters, but so does the system around it that makes progress observable and mistakes recoverable.

r002.rationale: It names shared capabilities such as understanding goals, planning, tool use, and adapting, but does not identify cross-domain reasoning as the shared foundation.

r003.rationale: It discusses adapting feedback mechanisms and automation, but says nothing about changing the final stage of post-training.
